explain.say: For about 95 percent of our species' history, everyone lived by hunting, fishing and gathering. Then, from about 11,500 years ago, people in several places began to farm. The archaeologist V. Gordon Childe called it the Neolithic Revolution in the 1930s. Look at the board: why would anyone give up foraging?

explain.say: Start with the first cause. The last Ice Age ended about 11,700 years ago, and a warmer, steadier climate let wild wheat and barley spread across the Fertile Crescent, the arc from Iraq to Turkey and the Levant. People who gathered them began to plant them. Which crop do you eat every day that began as a wild grass?

explain.say: Here is the surprise: farming was invented several times, separately. Look at the map. Wheat and barley in the Fertile Crescent, rice and millet in China, maize in Mexico, potatoes in the Andes of Peru, taro and bananas in New Guinea, sorghum in Africa's Sahel. Why is several separate inventions such strong evidence?

Now the last cause. At Göbekli Tepe in Turkey, people built huge carved stone circles about 11,600 years ago, before farming. Some archaeologists think feasts there pushed people to grow more grain. So did religion come first, or farming? What do you think?

explain.say: Was it progress? See the debate. Jared Diamond called farming the worst mistake in human history, pointing to shorter, sicker skeletons, and James C. Scott's Against the Grain, 2017, linked grain to taxes and states. Great thinking. Exam tip: say revolution only with care, because the change took thousands of years.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: Farming fed more people, not always better.

faq.a: The shift from foraging to farming and herding, with settled villages, which began about 11,500 years ago in the Fertile Crescent and separately in other regions. V. Gordon Childe coined the term in the 1930s.

Historians and archaeologists see several causes working together: a warmer, stable climate after the Ice Age, the spread of wild cereals, settled villages, growing populations and possibly feasting and ritual. No single cause explains every region.
asks: What caused the shift to agriculture?

faq.a: In at least seven regions independently: the Fertile Crescent, China, Mesoamerica, the Andes, New Guinea, Africa's Sahel and eastern North America. Farming then spread from these centres.
A site in south-east Turkey with huge carved stone pillars set in circles, built from about 11,600 years ago by people who did not yet farm. It suggests large gatherings and ritual came very early.

Mixed. Farming fed far more people and led to towns, writing and states, but early farmers were often shorter and less healthy than foragers, worked hard, caught diseases from animals and faced new inequality.

facts: Farming began in the Fertile Crescent about 11,500 years ago.
Göbekli Tepe in Turkey dates from about 11,600 years ago, before farming.
Maize was domesticated from a wild grass called teosinte in Mexico about 9,000 years ago.

quiz.say: Which crop was first domesticated in Mexico?
quiz.why: Maize was domesticated from teosinte in south-west Mexico about 9,000 years ago.

wrong.1: Rice was first domesticated in China.
wrong.2: Wheat began in the Fertile Crescent.

quiz.say: Why does Göbekli Tepe surprise archaeologists?
quiz.why: Its monumental pillars were raised by people who did not yet farm, reversing the old idea that farming came first.

wrong.1: It was a ritual site, not a city with homes and streets.
wrong.2: Writing came about 6,000 years later in Mesopotamia.
